Tree data structure. A connected acyclic graph, a hierarchical data structure with one distinguished root node from which all other nodes are reachable via a unique path. Each non-root node has exactly one parent node. A node may have zero or more children. Nodes with no children are leaf nodes. Nodes with at least one child are internal nodes. Trees are pervasive in computer science. File systems organize directories in trees. Compilers parse code into abstract syntax trees. Databases use B-trees and AVL trees for fast lookup. Recursion naturally mirrors tree structure.

Fundamental concepts establish the structure. A tree with n nodes has exactly n minus one edges and is connected and acyclic. Adding any edge creates a cycle. Removing any edge disconnects it. The height of a tree is the longest path from root to leaf. A tree with one node has height zero. The depth of a node is its distance from the root. The root has depth zero. A subtree rooted at node v consists of v and all its descendants and is itself a tree.

Binary trees restrict the structure further. Each node has at most two children, left and right. A full binary tree has each node with zero or two children. A complete binary tree fills levels left-to-right. A balanced binary tree has height O of log n, allowing operations like search and insertion in O of log n time. Binary search trees maintain the property that the left child is less than the parent, which is less than the right child. This enables efficient sorted traversal and lookup.

Tree traversals access nodes in different orders. Inorder visits left, then node, then right. It is useful for extracting sorted values from a binary search tree. Preorder visits node, then left, then right. It is natural for copying or serializing trees. Postorder visits left, then right, then node. It is natural for deletion or computing tree properties bottom-up. Breadth-first or level-order visits nodes by depth, useful for many algorithms.

Special trees serve specific purposes. Balanced search trees like AVL and red-black maintain height O of log n after insertion and deletion, guaranteeing O of log n operations. Heaps, specifically binary heaps, are partially ordered trees supporting O of log n insertion and O of one min or max extraction. Tries store strings where each node is a character and paths spell words. They are used in autocomplete and spell-checking. Segment trees and Fenwick trees are specialized structures for range queries and updates in O of log n.

Trees are among the most fundamental data structures in all of computer science. The tree abstraction appears whenever you need hierarchy: organizational charts, taxonomies, parse trees in compilers, game decision trees in AI, and file systems. Many advanced algorithms exploit tree structure to achieve efficiency: Huffman coding, closest-pair-in-divide-and-conquer, and dynamic programming on trees.
